    The batch annotation app

    Source: vignettes/shiny-workflow.Rmd
    shiny-workflow.Rmd

    Annotating one image is a job for at_project() and the ROI constructors. Annotating a queue of images — a plate of serial sections, a batch of slides, a folder of cubes — is what the annotation app is for. It wraps a Shiny app and a self-contained HTML5 canvas around a resumable session, so you can work through many images without losing your place, your labels, or your unsaved edits. at_app() builds the app as an ordinary shiny.appobj from explicit arguments (for embedding or testing), and at_annotate() launches it.

    Building a session

    A session is a queue of image paths plus a shared annotation template. Build one explicitly with at_session(), or grab a ready-made one for experimentation with at_example_session(), which copies the bundled tissue image into a temporary directory so the queue has real files to iterate.

    sess <- at_example_session(3)
sess
#> <annot_session>
#> images: 3  |  complete: 0  |  cursor: 1
#> out_dir: /tmp/RtmpGJku0b/hyperannotatR-example-session-33de3db71bee  |  autosave: TRUE

    Every image starts with status "pending", the cursor sits on the first image, and per-image projects are materialised lazily — nothing is read from disk until you visit it.

    Layer templates and label vocabularies

    Two things are shared across the whole queue. The label vocabulary is the flat list of allowed labels, bound to the number keys 1–9. The layer template is a list of at_layer() objects — with styles from at_style() — stamped onto every image the first time you open it, so each slide starts with the same empty layers ready to receive ROIs.

    regions <- at_layer("regions", labels = c("tumour", "necrosis", "stroma"),
                    style = at_style(colour = "#E64B35", fill_alpha = 0.3))
lesions <- at_layer("lesions", labels = c("focus", "margin"),
                    style = at_style(colour = "#4DBBD5", z = 2))

paths <- at_session_status(sess)$path
templated <- at_session(paths,
                        labels = c("tumour", "necrosis", "stroma", "focus", "margin"),
                        layers = list(regions, lesions),
                        out_dir = tempdir())

at_layers(at_current(templated))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 6
#>   name    n_rois labels    visible locked     z
#>   <chr>    <int> <list>    <lgl>   <lgl>  <int>
#> 1 regions      0 <chr [3]> TRUE    FALSE      1
#> 2 lesions      0 <chr [2]> TRUE    FALSE      2

    Launching the app

    With a session in hand, launch the application. This opens a browser and blocks, so it is never run inside a vignette:

    at_annotate(templated)

    at_annotate() is forgiving about its first argument: pass a session, a project, an image, a vector of paths, a directory, or NULL to open the bundled example.

    To embed the app, or to exercise it in tests without a browser, build the app object instead. Nothing is passed through global options:

    app <- at_app(session = templated, read_only = FALSE)
class(app)
#> [1] "shiny.appobj"

    Hyperspectral cubes in the app

    For spectral cubes the Display panel switches the canvas between natural colour, a single band, a pseudo-RGB / false-colour triple and the registered band operations listed by at_band_operations() (ratio, normalised difference, band means). These are display products: masks, spectra and exports always use the original cube values. The Cube table shows the image kind, wavelength range and gaps, value unit, calibration state, plane and how many bytes have been read. The probe tool picks a pixel whose spectrum appears on the Summary page next to ROI and layer spectra, and Download region exports the raw values of a selected ROI, the current view or custom bounds as an ENVI cube with provenance.

    Staged changes and status

    Annotations proposed by a partner package, such as a qupflowR handoff imported on the Data page or a control command, arrive as a staged patch. The Annotate page lists its creates, updates and conflicts; reviewed or locked ROIs are never changed automatically. Commit or discard it explicitly. One badge next to the save controls always shows the state (read-only, unsaved, staged, committed or saved), followed by a line with the time and folder of the last checkpoint, or a warning when that folder is temporary. See vignette("partner-interop") for the contract behind this.

    Keyboard shortcuts

    The canvas is built for speed, so almost everything has a key. Pick a layer and a label (radio buttons, or a digit for the label), draw, then commit and advance; Undo, Redo and Copy previous are also buttons next to the tools. Shortcuts are inactive while a text field, list, button or link has focus (label and layer radios keep them), while a dialog is open, and, except for ?, away from the Annotate page. The table below is the one the app shows when you press ?:

    Key Action
    Arrows / Shift+arrows canvas cursor: 1 / 10 image pixels
    Enter / Space point/rectangle anchors; polygon: Space vertices, Enter finish
    Escape cancel unfinished drawing/edit
    n / p next / previous image
    N next pending image
    1-9 select label
    q w e r t y tool: pan/rect/polygon/freehand/circle/point
    d delete last ROI
    Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Shift+Z undo / redo
    Shift+Enter save, mark complete & advance
    Shift+V paste previous image’s ROIs
    f flag image
    s save session
    Ctrl+E open export
    ? shortcut help

    Drawing also works without a mouse. Tab to the canvas: the arrow keys move a cursor by 1 level-0 image pixel (10 with Shift), Enter or Space places a point and starts or finishes a rectangle, Space places polygon vertices and Enter finishes the polygon after at least three, and Escape cancels an unfinished drawing or edit. A new shape is drawn dashed until the server accepts it. Drawing needs an active label and an unlocked layer; otherwise the app warns and no shape is added.

    The canvas shows a downsampled overview of the image (at most 2048 pixels on its longest side) with pan and zoom; it does not stream pyramid tiles. Drawing coordinates are always level-0 image pixels. Encoding the canvas image needs magick: TIFF reading can use tiff, but PNG images, including the tissue example, need magick. A missing capability or an image that fails to decode is reported before drawing is enabled, and navigation keeps working when the current image fails.

    Label colours, layer visibility, opacity, stroke width and z-order control the display. Hidden layers are neither drawn nor hit-tested on the canvas, but they still take part in masks and exports: visibility is not an analytical filter. Locked layers and protected imported ROIs cannot be edited or removed through the canvas, the keyboard, the ROI table or undo/redo, and labels cannot be added to a locked layer. These protections apply in the app; the R functions can still edit everything.

    Copy-forward for serial sections

    Adjacent serial sections often share most of their anatomy. Rather than redraw it, press Shift+V to copy the previous image’s ROIs into the unlocked layers of the current one, then use the edit tool to move whole regions into place. Combined with Shift+Enter (commit and advance), a run of near-identical sections can be annotated in a few keystrokes each.

    Autosave and recovery

    With autosave = TRUE (the default), the app writes the session to _session.rds in its out_dir after every annotation change. The badge shows saved only after the checkpoint has been written. A failed save leaves the current edits marked unsaved and keeps the previous valid checkpoint; press s to retry. With autosave = FALSE, navigation keeps edits in memory and the indicator stays unsaved until a save succeeds. Resume the last successful checkpoint with at_resume().

    Each new session gets its own temporary output directory, which R deletes when it exits, and the app warns about it; for real work pass a persistent out_dir to at_session() or at_annotate(). In scripts, at_save_session() refuses to replace an existing checkpoint unless you pass overwrite = TRUE, also when you omit path; app autosave asks for replacement explicitly. Before the app first replaces an existing _session.rds that holds another queue, or ROIs the new checkpoint lacks, it keeps a timestamped _session-*.previous.rds copy.

    All browser tabs of one app object share its in-memory queue, so reloading the page or opening a second tab continues from the latest edits; two tabs editing the same image keep the last edit. Loading another folder on the Data page writes the new queue into its own subfolder and keeps the previous queue, including its unsaved annotations and history, so Restore previous queue can bring it back. That recovery copy lives only in the running app: restore and save it before closing. An app attached to a control service refuses folder loads; the controller loads sessions instead.

    The Data page reads folder and handoff paths on the machine running R: the app is meant for local use. For any shared deployment, set options(hyperannotatR.app_root = "/allowed/folder") so the app refuses paths outside that folder.

    sess <- at_set_status(sess, 1, "complete")
sess <- at_next(sess)

at_save_session(sess)
recovered <- at_resume(file.path(sess$out_dir, "_session.rds"))
recovered
#> <annot_session>
#> images: 3  |  complete: 1  |  cursor: 2
#> out_dir: /tmp/RtmpGJku0b/hyperannotatR-example-session-33de3db71bee  |  autosave: TRUE

    The cursor, statuses, materialised projects, and templates all come back intact.

    File-backed images are saved as a versioned source descriptor (the canonical source path, backend and reader options), not as pixels, and are reopened when needed; keep the original source files available. In-memory images keep their only pixel copy. A session whose sources are unavailable still loads, with its annotations intact.

    at_inspect_saved("annotations/_session.rds")
project <- at_current(recovered)
at_inspect_source(project)
project <- at_relink_source(project, "/new/location/original.tif")
recovered$projects[[recovered$cursor]] <- project
at_save_session(recovered, overwrite = TRUE)

    Relinking explicitly accepts a replacement source after checking its size, pyramid levels, bands and wavelengths. For readers with non-default options, pass options = list(...) when an old file does not record them. The saved source signature compares file size and modification time (for ENVI cubes, of both the header and the data file): it detects many replacements but cannot prove identical content. Changed source metadata needs explicit relinking.

    Queue entries saved without identifiers are migrated by their recorded row position; existing valid identifiers and geometry are kept. Older lightweight images reopen through the known default readers, and inspection reports that their reader options were inferred. Ambiguous identities and unsupported schemas are refused; at_inspect_saved() reports such issues without modifying the file.

    App checkpoints write complete, uniquely named project files before replacing the session file, and keep the project files that older checkpoints refer to. On Unix the replacement is a checked rename in the same directory; on Windows the previous file is backed up and restored if an ordinary write fails. Neither guarantees durability across a power loss. Do not delete retained project files while a checkpoint still refers to them.

    The session API without the app

    Everything the canvas does to a session is available as plain functions, which is what makes batches scriptable and testable. Inspect the queue with at_session_status(), walk it with at_next() / at_prev() / at_goto(), and read a richer progress report — one column per label — with at_manifest().

    at_session_status(sess)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 9
#>     idx entry_id              export_stem path  name  status project_path n_rois
#>   <int> <chr>                 <chr>       <chr> <chr> <chr>  <chr>         <int>
#> 1     1 entry_at_33de4e1ffe8… entry_at_3… /tmp… imag… compl… NA                0
#> 2     2 entry_at_33de4e1ffe8… entry_at_3… /tmp… imag… pendi… NA                0
#> 3     3 entry_at_33de4e1ffe8… entry_at_3… /tmp… imag… pendi… NA                0
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: modified <dttm>

at_manifest(sess)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 11
#>     idx entry_id  export_stem name  path  status n_layers n_rois tumour necrosis
#>   <int> <chr>     <chr>       <chr> <chr> <chr>     <int>  <int>  <int>    <int>
#> 1     1 entry_at… entry_at_3… imag… /tmp… compl…        0      0      0        0
#> 2     2 entry_at… entry_at_3… imag… /tmp… pendi…        0      0      0        0
#> 3     3 entry_at… entry_at_3… imag… /tmp… pendi…        0      0      0        0
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: stroma <int>

    Use these to seed a session programmatically, pre-fill statuses, or audit progress in a report — no Shiny required.

    Export scoping

    The export panel (Ctrl+E) writes the selected formats (an integer TIFF mask with its legend sidecar, GeoJSON, QuPath GeoJSON, and an ROI table as CSV) for a scope: the current image, every image marked complete, every flagged image, or the whole queue. The current image is exported from the live project, other entries from the session’s stored projects, and every layer is included; the app has no layer selector. Scope all includes flagged and skipped images, so choose complete when only reviewed annotations should leave the session. The zip download holds every complete bundle plus the receipt, and a copy is written to the session’s export folder. The receipt lists complete files, skips and errors; check it before assuming that every requested image and format succeeded. To export a subset of layers, call the writers from R instead: at_write_geojson(), at_write_qupath() and at_mask() take a layer argument.

    Those export formats — and how hyperannotatR round-trips with QuPath, GeoJSON, and mask TIFFs — are the subject of the next vignette, “Interoperability”.
